brief: 6 typefaces with stories so good you'll use them on purpose for the rest of your life.

slots.body: Fonts carry history, rebellion, and purpose in every letterform. Here are six you will use on purpose forever.

slots.title: The Original Old Style
slots.body: Claude Garamond cut punches in sixteenth-century Paris. His letterforms survived wars, revolutions, and digital obsolescence to remain the quiet king of readability.
slots.quote: Old style never dies; it simply waits for good designers.

slots.title: A Geometric Modernist
slots.body: Paul Renner drew Futura in 1927 as a manifesto for the machine age. In 1969, it left Earth on the Apollo 11 plaque, etching modernism into lunar dust.
slots.quote: Function can be as romantic as poetry.

slots.title: The Transitional Serif
slots.body: John Baskerville’s obsessive contrast and crisp serifs outraged eighteenth-century printers. Benjamin Franklin loved it so much he smuggled punches back to America.

slots.title: The Ubiquitous Swiss Classic
slots.body: Born as Neue Haas Grotesk in 1957, Helvetica became the voice of corporations, subway systems, and protest posters. Neutral, yes. Invisible, never.

slots.title: America’s First Serif Voice
slots.body: William Caslon’s sturdy serifs printed the Declaration of Independence. When doubt strikes, designers still whisper the old rule: When in doubt, use Caslon.

slots.title: The World’s Most Hated
slots.body: Vincent Connare designed Comic Sans for a Microsoft Bob speech bubble in 1994. It was never meant for gravestones, yet it became an unlikely populist icon.
slots.quote: Every font has a place if the story fits.

slots.body: Stop letting algorithms choose your voice. Build a typographic toolkit that carries meaning, history, and intent.
